Data: [TidyTuesday 2026-08-18](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-08-18).

The IELTS Academic paper is reported as a distribution, one share per band, and almost every use of it is a single number: a university asks for 6.5, an employer asks for 7, and the mean band of a country is quoted as though it settled the matter.
The left panel keeps the whole distribution and orders the 40 nationalities by that mean, and two things move together.
The mass climbs, which is what the ordering is for, and it also tightens: the correlation between a nationality's mean band and the spread around it is −0.42.
The United Arab Emirates, at 5.52, spreads its candidates across five bands that each hold at least a tenth, and needs four of them to cover half.
Germany, the highest of the 40 at 7.57, covers half its candidates in two, and puts more than a third on one band alone.

The right panel is what that costs a reader who stops at the mean.
Hong Kong and Ghana share a mean band of 6.63, to two decimals, out of 40 nationalities.
Ghana sends 70.8% of its candidates over 6.5 and Hong Kong 62.2%, a gap of more than eight points hidden inside an identical average.
Ghana covers half its candidates in two bands and Hong Kong needs four, and the tail is where the two really part: 7.1% of Hong Kong candidates come out below 5.5, against 2.5% of Ghana's.
Two countries, one average, and a different answer to the only question the number is usually asked to settle.

Three cautions.
The shares are of each nationality's own candidates and the data carries no candidate counts, so a country that sends a few hundred people counts as much here as one that sends hundreds of thousands, and nothing in the figure is a population estimate.
Bands below 4 arrive as one open bucket with no score of its own; it is drawn and averaged at 3.5, so every mean quoted here leans on that choice, though the bucket is small enough in most columns that the ordering barely moves without it.
The heaviest tiles are also cut off: the fill ramp tops out at 20% and 46 of the 480 tiles carry more than that, the heaviest being Germany at 34.7%, which keeps the middle of the range readable at the cost of flattening the top.
